questions.a: boxes, babies, knives, children, sheep. Wrong answers 'boxs/childs/sheeps' show rule-gaps at the hiss-sound, irregular, and unchanged steps respectively.

questions.q: Fix: 'I have many homeworks and two luggages.'
questions.a: 'much homework and two pieces of luggage' — both uncountable, no plurals. A wrong answer keeping the -s shows the student doesn't yet sort nouns into countable vs uncountable.

questions.q: 'The ___(mouse/mice) ate the cheese' vs 'All the ___ ran away.' Which form in each?
questions.a: First: mouse (one). Second: mice (many). A wrong answer 'mouses' or singular-for-plural shows the irregular form isn't yet automatic.

questions.q: Numbers: singular means one, plural means more than one — but English ______ in five ways: +s (books), +es (boxes), y→ies (cities), f→ves (leaves), irregular (children, feet, mice), and some never change (sheep, news).

Fill in the blank: Numbers: singular means one, plural means more than one — but English ______ in five ways: +s (books), +es (boxes), y→ies (cities), f→ves (leaves), irregular (children, feet, mice), and some never change (sheep, news).
Fill in the blank: Sort objects on the desk by ending: book+s, box+es (hiss-sounds s/x/ch/sh need es), city→cities (______+y drops y), leaf→leaves (f→v+es).
What is Numbers? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Numbers: singular means one, plural means more than one — but English pluralizes in five ways: +s (books), +es (boxes), y→ies (cities), f→ves (leaves), irregular (children, feet, mice), and some never change (sheep, news).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Numbers?
questions.a: Students apply +s universally → 'childs', 'mouses', 'foots' — and add -s to uncountables → 'waters', 'furnitures', 'homeworks'.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student forms plurals by the five rules, produces the irregular set from memory, and catches double-plural errors ('childs', 'sheeps', 'mices').
